expressions.name: E
expressions.equation: k_tri + k_norm * k_logt + k_list + k_list2 + k_bad + k_logn4

scenarios with distributions.name: Three climate scenarios
scenarios with distributions.description: The same model under three futures. `Climate` is a scenario index list: one of its indices is live at a time, chosen under Simulation on the left, and every block indexed by it is read at that one. So `Runoff` and `LakeVolume` hold a value per scenario while `Conc` — which reads the volume but is not itself scenario-indexed — is a single quantity. Switch the scenario and the whole model answers differently, where the usual arrangement is one simulation per scenario.

index_lists.name: Climate
index_lists.comment: Alternative futures, not an axis of the model: one runs at a time.

parameters.name: Runoff
parameters.comment: How fast the soil drains into the lake.

recorders with a spread.name: Peak dose and when it happened (spread)
recorders with a spread.description: A release pulse passes through a lake and out again. The five blocks that depend on what has already happened are all here: a discrete event fires when the concentration falls back past a limit, a min/max holds the peak dose, a snapshot remembers the year the limit was crossed, a running mean averages the dose from that year on, and a delay reports the dose a century earlier. Nothing here is a function of the state alone -- each one has to be recorded as the solver goes.

triggers.name: Below_limit
triggers.comment: The year the dose falls back through the limit on its way down.

lookup-driver with a spread.name: A time-dependent driver (spread)
lookup-driver with a spread.description: Two lookup tables drive the model: the groundwater flow through a biosphere object over a glacial cycle, and the lake area as the basin silts up. Both are read at the simulation clock, which is what makes a lookup table a time-dependent parameter rather than a constant. The advective transfer follows Q_gw / V, so its rate -- and the Jacobian -- move with time; the dose expression divides by the lake area, which is what the table is there to say.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.comment: Mean depth of the lake: area times this is its volume.

parameters.name: V_lake
parameters.comment: Lake volume, so the groundwater flow becomes a turnover rate.

lookups.name: Q_gw
lookups.comment: Groundwater flow through the object. Nearly stops under permafrost, between 9000 and 12000 years.

lookups.name: Area_lake
lookups.comment: Lake surface area. The basin silts up: by 16000 years only a small pond is left.

thermostat with a spread.name: A thermostat switching a heater (spread)
thermostat with a spread.description:
A room losing heat to 5 °C outside, with a time constant of two hours, and a heater that warms it at 10 °C an hour, switched by a thermostat with a dead band: on when the room falls through 19 °C, off when it rises through 21 °C. Between switches the room follows Newton's law of cooling. At each switch the right-hand side jumps, and the solver has to stop exactly there rather than step across it.

Too_cold and Too_warm are the two triggers. Each takes a snapshot of the time it fires (On_since, Off_since), and the heater is on while On_since is the later of the two: a memory of which way the room last crossed, made of two snapshots.

The switching times are known in closed form. Warming from 15 to 21 °C takes τ·ln(10/4) = 1.83 h; after that each cycle is τ·ln(16/14) = 0.27 h with the heater off and τ·ln(6/4) = 0.81 h with it on, 42 switches in the day. The run lands on every one of them to within half a millisecond.

bouncing-ball with a spread.name: Bouncing ball (spread)
bouncing-ball with a spread.description:
A ball thrown straight up from the floor at 20 m/s, falling back under gravity and bouncing with 0.9 of the speed it landed with: the classic test of how a solver handles events. Height is the one compartment. Bounce is a trigger that fires when Height falls through zero, so the solver stops exactly there and starts again. Each bounce takes two snapshots, its time (T_bounce) and the speed the ball leaves the floor with (V_up), and between bounces the ball's Velocity is V_up − g·(t − T_bounce).

The landing speed is read off the flight time: a flight from the floor and back takes 2V/g, so the ball lands at g times half its time in the air. That keeps V_up from reading its own value, which a snapshot may not do. The bounces come where the closed form (2·v0/g)·(1 − eⁿ)/(1 − e) puts them: 4.08, 7.75 and 11.05 s, and so on, twelve in the thirty seconds, with the energy falling to e² = 0.81 of itself at each.

Try: run it to 45 s. The bounces pile up towards (2·v0/g)/(1 − e) = 40.8 s, where infinitely many of them would happen in a finite time (Zeno behaviour). After about a hundred, the flights are too short to resolve and the ball falls through the floor. That is a property of the model, which needs a rule for coming to rest, not a fault in the solver.

four-compartment with a spread.name: Four-compartment test model (spread)
four-compartment with a spread.description: A four-compartment test model. C1 drains to C2 and C3, C2 feeds C3, and C3 discharges to C4. The Outflow expression is the discharge rate times C3, so the release curve can be read directly.

post-processing with a spread.name: Dose from a released inventory (spread)
post-processing with a spread.description: A model with no compartments. Nothing is integrated: the release to the biosphere is a measured series, and the concentration, the dose per nuclide and the total dose follow from it directly. Models of this shape are common — 15 of the 71 real projects this was measured against — and they are what the results of a transport calculation are turned into. The blocks are evaluated over the time span in dependency order, with the same clock a solved model would see.

parameters.name: Fraction
parameters.comment: Share of the release that reaches this recipient.

lookups.name: Release
lookups.comment: Release to the biosphere, from a transport calculation. Every nuclide shares the shape here; a real model gives each its own.

index_reductions.name: Dose_total
index_reductions.comment: Every nuclide together — the number an assessment reports.

index_reductions.name: Dose_worst
index_reductions.comment: The nuclide contributing most at each moment.

waste-packages with a spread.name: Canisters failing: a source term with barriers, and two disruptive events (spread)
waste-packages with a spread.description: 4,500 spent-fuel canisters in a repository. None fails before year 1,000; after that the failures follow a Weibull with a characteristic life of 50,000 years and a shape of 2, the corrosion form. When a canister fails, 3% of its caesium and 0.5% of the rest is in the water at once (the instant release fraction) and the remainder waits for the fuel matrix, which dissolves at one part in ten million a year. The release goes into the near-field water, which is flushed to the geosphere; switch the mass-balance audit on under SIMULATION to watch the bookkeeping close. Two disruptive events act on it: an earthquake, a Poisson process at 2e-5 a year that fails 5% of the still-intact canisters at each occurrence, and a glaciation at 100,000 years that strips 80% of the biosphere out of the model. A deterministic run takes the earthquake in its expected-value form; a probabilistic run draws its occurrences — compare the staircase of Quake with its expected line.

parameters.name: t_first_failure
parameters.comment: No canister fails before this: the time the earliest corrosion process could breach one.

parameters.name: canister_life
parameters.comment: The Weibull scale: 63% of the canisters have failed one life after the first failure.

parameters.name: matrix_rate
parameters.comment: The fraction of the exposed fuel matrix dissolving per year. Everything bound in it leaves congruently.

parameters.name: flush_rate
parameters.comment: Turnover of the near-field water: the fraction leaving for the geosphere per year.

parameters.name: geo_rate
parameters.comment: Transit through the geosphere to the biosphere, as a first-order rate.

parameters.name: quake_rate
parameters.comment: Earthquakes breaching canisters: one in fifty thousand years.

parameters.name: t_glacial
parameters.comment: When the next ice sheet reaches the site.

waste_packages.name: Canisters
waste_packages.comment: The source term: the inventory starts inside the canisters and reaches the water only as they fail and the fuel dissolves. What leaves is the line drawn out of the block.

compartments.name: NearField
compartments.comment: The water in and around the failed canisters. A solubility limit would go on the transfer out of here, as an availability.

transfers.name: Release
transfers.comment: What leaves the canisters. Its rate is the block itself, so there is nothing to set.

transfers.name: Loss
transfers.comment: Dilution and dispersal out of the modelled biosphere.

events.name: Quake
events.comment: An earthquake: at each occurrence 5% of the canisters still intact fail. Deterministically a hazard of 1e-6 a year on the intact inventory; in a probabilistic run, drawn occurrences.

events.name: Glaciation
events.comment: The ice sheet arrives: 80% of what the biosphere holds is scraped away, out of the model.
